# Targeting LRH-1 alleviates diabetes-induced lipotoxicity in podocytes: role of PLIN5-mediated lipid droplet turnover

**Authors:** Qian Guan; Zijing Zhu; Hongtu Hu; Juan Wang; Yanqin Fan; Peng Ye; Qian Yang; Guohua Ding; Jijia Hu

**Affiliations:** aDivision of Nephrology, Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan, China | bNephrology and Urology Research Institute of Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan, China | cDepartment of Nephrology, The Central Hospital of Wuhan, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China | dKey Laboratory for Molecular Diagnosis of Hubei Province, The Central Hospital of Wuhan, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China | eDivision of Urology, Shenzhen Hospital of Southern Medical University, Shenzhen, China

## Abstract

Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is characterized by podocyte injury driven by intracellular lipid accumulation. Liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1) is a key nuclear receptor regulating lipid metabolism, yet its role in podocyte lipotoxicity remains unclear. This study identifies the LRH-1/perilipin 5 (PLIN5) axis as a critical pathway for maintaining lipid homeostasis in podocytes and a promising pharmacological target for DKD. We demonstrated that hyperglycemia suppressed the LRH-1/PLIN5 axis, leading to lipid droplet accumulation, oxidative stress, and podocyte injury in db/db mice and cultured podocytes. Activation of LRH-1 with agonist 1,2-dilauroyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphocholine (DLPC) or its overexpression restored mitochondrial lipid utilization, reduced lysosomal lipotoxicity, and protected against renal injury by upregulating PLIN5. Furthermore, virtual screening of a natural product library identified chebulinic acid (CA) as a novel PLIN5-targeting agonist. CA treatment significantly upregulated PLIN5 expression, ameliorated lipid accumulation, and improved renal function in db/db mice. Our findings unveil the therapeutic potential of targeting the LRH-1/PLIN5 axis and present CA as a promising candidate for the treatment of diabetic podocytopathy.

## Abstract

This graphical abstract illustrates the central findings of the study: under diabetic conditions (high glucose), the expression of the nuclear receptor liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1) and its target, the lipid droplet (LD)-associated protein perilipin 5 (PLIN5), is suppressed in podocytes. This suppression disrupts LD turnover, leading to excessive LD accumulation, increased lysosomal lipolysis, and reduced mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation. The resulting lipotoxicity causes oxidative stress (ROS), lipid peroxidation (MDA), and ultimately, podocyte injury and diabetic kidney disease (DKD). The study demonstrates that therapeutic intervention using the LRH-1 agonist 1,2-dilauroyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphocholine (DLPC) or the PLIN5-targeting compound chebulinic acid restores the LRH-1/PLIN5 axis, promotes healthy LD–mitochondria interaction, alleviates lipotoxicity, and protects against podocyte injury and renal dysfunction.

## Introduction

Despite compelling evidence that podocyte injury is a key element in the pathogenesis of diabetic kidney disease (DKD), targeted therapies for podocyte injury remain limited in clinical practice [1,2]. Recent studies have shed light on the intricate link between podocyte lipid dysregulation and renal injury [3,4]. Our previous studies demonstrated that diabetes induced lipid accumulation in podocytes [5], suggesting that revealing the mechanism of lipid metabolism disorders in podocytes may provide critical therapeutic targets for patients with DKD.

Liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1), also known as nuclear receptor subfamily 5 group A member 2 (NR5A2), is a crucial orphan nuclear receptor that serves as a master regulator of lipid, glucose, and amino acid metabolism [6,7]. Evidence indicates that hyperglycemia diminishes LRH-1 expression, a reduction that is pivotal in driving metabolic dysfunction [8]. LRH-1 governs fatty acid synthesis, oxidation, transport, and cholesterol metabolism through precise gene expression modulation, thereby influencing energy metabolism and lipid accumulation within kidney cells [8–10]. Furthermore, LRH-1 maintains glucose balance and normal kidney function by regulating glycogen synthesis and glycolysis pathways [11,12]. While LRH-1 is known to be protective against renal metabolic stress, the specific downstream effectors it recruits to manage lipid flux in the podocyte remain to be fully elucidated.

A potential candidate for this regulation is perilipin 5 (PLIN5), a protein that plays a vital role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis and preventing lipotoxicity [13]. In the podocyte, lipid droplets (LDs) serve as dynamic organelles that sequester free fatty acids (FFAs) to prevent cellular damage; however, pathological LDs accumulation – as seen in DKD – indicates a failure in lipid turnover. PLIN5 coats these LDs and modulates the interaction between lipids and lipases, thereby tightly regulating the rate of lipid breakdown (lipolysis) [14]. By controlling lipase access to the LDs core, PLIN5 facilitates the controlled release of fatty acids for mitochondrial energy production, a process critical for maintaining the high metabolic demands of the glomerular filtration barrier [15,16]. Alterations in PLIN5 expression are linked to various metabolic disorders, including obesity and fatty liver disease [17–19]. Recent studies have indicated that PLIN5 is expressed in renal cells and is involved in renal lipid metabolism [20]. Importantly, emerging findings in hepatic models suggest that PLIN5 might be a novel target of LRH-1 to mobilize LDs and protect tissues from lipid overload [21]. However, whether PLIN5 serves as the primary downstream mediator of LRH-1 in podocytes under diabetic conditions, and how this axis contributes to the progression of DKD, remains unclear.

In this study, we hypothesized that LRH-1 alleviates podocyte lipotoxicity by enhancing PLIN5-dependent LD turnover. We defined the role of the LRH-1/PLIN5 axis in coordinating LD–mitochondrial dynamics using both in vivo and in vitro diabetic models. These findings not only clarify the mechanism of lipotoxicity in the kidney but also identify a pharmacologically targetable axis for the treatment of DKD.

## Methods

### Reagents

#### Reagents

Rabbit anti-LRH-1 antibodies and rabbit anti-PLIN5 antibodies were obtained from Proteintech (Wuhan, China); mouse anti-Wilms’ tumor 1 (WT1) antibodies were purchased from Novus (Centennial, CO); mouse anti-Lamp1 antibodies were purchased from Progen Biotechnik (Heidelberg, Germany); anti-β-actin mouse monoclonal antibody, fluorescent secondary antibodies were purchased from Antgene (Wuhan, China). 1,2-Dilauroyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphocholine (DLPC), tetragalloylglucose, cistanoside A, chebulinic acid (CA), tubuloside A, and poliumoside were purchased from MedChemExpress (Shanghai, China), dissolved in glycolic acid (GC) at 23 °C, and kept at −20 °C. LRH-1 pcDNA plasmid and control plasmid were obtained from GenePharma (Shanghai, China). BODIPY 493/503 was purchased from Qiyue Bioengineering (Xi’an, China). MitoTracker was purchased from MedChemExpress (Shanghai, China). Lipid peroxidation (malondialdehyde, MDA) assay was purchased from Jiancheng Bioengineering (Nanjing, China). Lipofectamine 3000 transfection reagent was obtained from Invitrogen (Waltham, MA). The Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay System (E1910) and passive lysis buffer were purchased from Promega (Madison, WI). LysoTracker (catalog no. L7528) and MitoTracker Deep Red (catalog no. M22426) were obtained from Invitrogen (Waltham, MA). Dihydroethidium (DHE) was purchased from Invitrogen (Waltham, MA), and H2‑DCFDA and JC-1 were obtained from Beyotime (Shanghai, China).

### db/db mice and treatment

Twelve-week-old male db/db mice and genetic control db/+ mice were obtained from Cavens Laboratory (Changzhou, China). Mice were housed under standard SPF conditions (12 h light, 22 ± 2 °C, 3/cage, food/water ad libitum) with daily welfare monitoring; humane endpoints were set but not reached. Mice were monitored for body weight and urinary protein levels in DKD mice for a period of 20 weeks. For LRH-1 agonist treatment, mice were treated daily by oral gavage with DLPC (100 mg/kg) dissolved in GC, or with an equal volume of GC alone (vehicle) for 3 weeks. For CA treatment, a preliminary dose-finding experiment was first conducted to determine the appropriate dose. db/db mice were randomly assigned to a vehicle control group or CA treatment groups at 3, 10, and 20 mg/kg (i.p., daily for 1 week; n = 6 per group). Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and glomerular PLIN5 expression were measured as primary readouts. The 10 mg/kg dose significantly reduced UACR and upregulated PLIN5 expression (both p < 0.01), whereas the 3 mg/kg dose showed only modest non-significant effects, and the 20 mg/kg dose provided no additional benefit over 10 mg/kg (p > 0.05). Based on the principle of the minimum effective dose (Supplementary Figure S1), 10 mg/kg was selected for subsequent formal experiments. In the efficacy study, db/db mice received CA (10 mg/kg) or vehicle by daily intraperitoneal injection for three consecutive weeks [22]. No mice died during the treatment period. On the last day of week 20, the animals were placed in a metabolic chamber to collect 24-h urine. Mice were sacrificed by cardiac puncture after they were anesthetized with chloral hydrate (400 mg/kg). The kidneys were collected for subsequent examination. The quantitative and statistical results are presented in Figure 1(A,B). Podocyte foot process width was quantified based on transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images. Briefly, TEM images of glomerular tissue were acquired at a magnification of ×10,000, and ImageJ software (v1.8.0, Bethesda, MD) was used for measurement. For each animal (n = 3 per group), at least 20-foot processes were randomly selected, and a straight line perpendicular to the long axis of the foot process was drawn to measure the width; the mean value per animal was used for group analysis (Supplementary Figure S2). Two independent observers performed the measurement to avoid subjective bias, and the average value was taken as the final foot process width. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 7 software (La Jolla, CA), and data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) (n = 3 per group). Randomization used a random number table. Treatments and assessments were performed in a fixed order (vehicle first, then treated groups) to minimize bias.

*Figure 1.: DKD mouse model of db/db was established to confirm glomerular podocyte injury. (A) Body weight of different groups of mice at week 20. (B) Blood glucose of different groups of mice at week 20. (C) Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) in different groups of mice (n = 6). (D) Representative periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining in glomerulus from renal tissues (n = 6). (E) Glomerular sclerosis index of the PAS staining (n = 6). (F) Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observation of the DKD mouse podocyte foot processes. (G, H) Representative immunofluorescence staining (WT1-positive podocytes) in glomerulus from renal tissues (n = 6). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01. Five visual fields for each section analyzed. (I) Quantification of foot process width (FPW): the db/db group showed a significantly wider foot process width (0.33 ± 0.12 μm) compared to the db/m control group (0.16 ± 0.08 μm; unpaired Student’s t-test, p < 0.01). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01 vs. db/m group. Scale bar, 1 μM (white).*

### Cell cultures and treatments

A cell line of conditionally immortalized human podocytes (HPCs) was obtained from Dr. Moin A. Saleem (Academic Renal Unit, Southmead Hospital, Bristol, UK). The HPCs were cultured using the method previously described [5]. Specifically, HPCs were cultured in RPMI-1640 basal medium (HyClone, Logan, UT) supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, Waltham, MA), penicillin G (100 IU/mL), streptomycin (100 μg/mL), and 1× insulin–transferrin–selenium (ITS; Invitrogen, Waltham, MA) at 33 °C for proliferation. Then, they were thermoswitched to 37 °C for 12 days without ITS to induce differentiation. All experiments were conducted with differentiated cells. Differentiated podocytes were exposed to high glucose (HG, 30 mM d-glucose) or osmotic control (30 mM d-mannitol) for 24 h. For CA treatment, cells were incubated with 10 µM CA for 24 h with HG exposure.

### Western immunoblotting

Cells or tissues (isolated glomeruli) were collected with RIPA buffer. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and then transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore Corp., Burlington, MA). The membranes were then incubated with a primary antibody (LRH-1 1:1,000, PLIN5 1:1,000, β-actin 1:5,000) in 5% milk overnight at 4 °C. Next, the membranes were labeled with an Alexa Fluor 680/790-labeled (1:10,000, LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE) goat anti-mouse/goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody, followed by scanning via an LI-COR Odyssey Infrared Imaging System.

### Immunofluorescence (IF) assay

The frozen kidney sections were blocked and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by incubation with fluorescent secondary antibodies at 37 °C for 90 min in the dark. The nuclei were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI, Antgene, Wuhan, China) for 5 min. All microscopic images were detected with a fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan).

### Immunohistochemical assay

Renal tissues from mice were embedded in paraffin, and then 4-μm tissue sections were prepared. Tissue sections were subjected to deparaffinization, rehydration, antigen retrieval, and blocking. Subsequently, sections were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. Then, the sections were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody for 30 min. After washing, samples were stained with diaminobenzidine for 5 min and counterstained in hematoxylin. Slides were examined by microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan).

### Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lipid peroxidation MDA content assessment

The production of ROS in glomeruli and podocytes was assessed using the DHE (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA) and 2′,7′-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (H2-DCFDA, Beyotime, Shanghai, China) assays, respectively. Mitochondrial membrane potential was analyzed by staining with JC-1 (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). To detect podocyte lipid metabolites, the lipid peroxidation (MDA) Assay (A003) was employed. The sample and standard were treated with TBA solution, incubated at 95 °C for 60 min, cooled in an ice bath for 10 min, and then transferred to a microplate for final microspectrograph analysis.

### LDs and live-cell dye imaging and quantification

Cells were seeded onto six-well chambered coverslips and grown in HPCs growth media. For MitoTracker and LysoTracker experiments, live cells were pretreated with 200 nM LysoTracker (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, catalog no. L7528) and/or 200 nM MitoTracker Deep Red (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, catalog no. M22426) 3 h before experimental endpoint. At experimental endpoint, media were aspirated, and wells were washed in PBS followed by fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) (Alfa Aesar, Ward Hill, MA, catalog no. J61899AP) for 10 min at RT. Cells were then incubated with BODIPY 493/503 (1 μg/mL; Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, catalog no. D3922) for 20 min, washed 1× with DPBS, and mounted with Ibidi mounting medium with DAPI (Ibidi, catalog no. 50011). All images were collected using a 63× oil-immersion objective on a Leica TCS SP8 laser scanning confocal microscope (Wetzlar, Germany). Ten to 15 representative images were obtained for each well. Quantification of BODIPY-positive LDs was performed using ImageJ software (Bethesda, MD). An ImageJ macro was written to autothreshold and quantify LDs/nuclei for all images.

### Nucleic acid–protein docking

Molecular docking was conducted to validate the binding interactions between proteins and nucleic acids. The HDOCK online platform (http://hdock.phys.hust.edu.cn/) was used for this procedure. HDOCK facilitates the analysis of protein–protein and protein–nucleic acid docking in various conformations, assessing binding activity and interaction distances within 5 Å of interacting residues. The nucleic acid sequence was obtained from the NCBI database, and the human PLIN5 protein structure was downloaded from UniProt. The LRH-1 nucleic acid sequence was modeled using the 3DRNA server. Protein–nucleic acid interactions were visualized using PyMOL software (Version 4.3.0).

### Virtual screening in natural product libraries

The virtual screening process was conducted by MedChemExpress (MCE, Monmouth Junction, NJ). In conclusion, the structure of the human PLIN5 protein was obtained from the RCSB PDB database. Subsequently, the two-dimensional format of the compounds in the Natural Products Library Plus was optimized and converted to three-dimensional mode using Schrödinger Maestro 12.8 software (schrodinger.com) and PyMOL 4.3.0 software (PYMOL.org/). The top 200 PLIN5 protein-targeting candidates were identified using the virtual screening workflow module.

### Ethical approval statement

All experimental protocols involving laboratory animals were reviewed and approved by the Laboratory Animal Welfare & Ethics Committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University (Approval No. 2020306). The study was conducted in accordance with the Guidelines for the Ethical Use of Laboratory Animals issued by the National Health Commission of China and the International Guiding Principles for Biomedical Research Involving Animals.

### Dual luciferase reporter assay

To verify the transcriptional regulation of PLIN5 by LRH-1 through the predicted GTCATT binding motif in the PLIN5 promoter region, a dual luciferase (LUC) reporter assay was performed. Differentiated HPCs (induced at 37 °C for 12 days) were seeded into 24-well plates at a density of 5 × 104 cells per well and cultured overnight in complete medium at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 humidified atmosphere. When cells reached 70–80% confluence, they were co-transfected with three plasmids using Lipofectamine 3000 reagent (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol: 500 ng of firefly LUC reporter plasmid (either wild‑type PLIN5 promoter construct or a mutant construct in which the GTCATT motif was mutated to GCCATT), 1 μg of LRH-1 overexpression vector (pcDNA3.1‑LRH1) or empty pcDNA3.1 vector (as negative control), and 50 ng of Renilla LUC reporter plasmid (pRL‑TK, Promega, Madison, WI) as an internal control for transfection efficiency. Forty-eight hours after transfection, the medium was discarded, and cells were washed twice with ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Then, 100 μL of 1× passive lysis buffer (Promega, Madison, WI) was added to each well, and cells were lysed by gentle shaking at room temperature for 15 min. The lysates were collected, and firefly and Renilla LUC activities were measured sequentially using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Assay System (Promega, Madison, WI, E1910) on a GloMax 96 Microplate Luminometer (Promega, Madison, WI) following the kit instructions.

Relative LUC activity was calculated as the ratio of firefly LUC activity to Renilla LUC activity. All experiments were performed in triplicate wells, and each independent experiment was repeated at least three times. Data are expressed as mean ± SD.

### Public ChIP-seq data processing

Publicly available LRH-1 (NR5A2) ChIP-seq datasets were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession numbers GSM1143122, GSM1505693, and GSM1505694 (Supplementary Figure S3). Raw FASTQ files were processed using fastp (v0.22.0) to remove adapters and low-quality bases, followed by alignment to the human reference genome (hg38) using Bowtie2 (v2.2.5) with the very-sensitive parameter. Duplicate reads were removed using Picard MarkDuplicates (v2.18.29). Normalized BigWig tracks were generated using deepTools bamCoverage (v3.5.4) with RPKM normalization. Peak calling was performed using MACS2 (v2.2.7.1) in narrow peak mode (q-value < 0.05). Quality control was performed to ensure NSC > 1.05, RSC > 0.8, and unique mapped reads > 10 million.

### Statistics

At least three experiments were conducted with 3–6 replicates per assay. Quantitative data were expressed as means ± SEM. Continuous variables for two groups were compared using Student’s t-tests. Continuous variables for more than two groups were compared using a one-way ANOVA test. Statistical analyses of the data were performed using GraphPad Prism (Version 7.0, La Jolla, CA). A p value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results

### Establishment of mouse models of diabetic nephropathy and renal phenotypes

To investigate the role of LRH-1 and PLIN5 in diabetic podocyte lipid metabolism, we used db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes with progressive kidney injury (Figure 1(A,B)). The renal phenotype of the db/db mice was characterized by a significant increase in the UACR (Figure 1(C)). Morphological changes were assessed using TEM and periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining (Figure 1(D–F)). TEM revealed significant foot processes effacement of podocytes (Figure 1(G)), expansion of the mesangial matrix, and marked sclerosis of glomeruli in db/db mice. Furthermore, there was a significantly decreasing number of podocytes in each glomerulus, as evidenced by a lower count of WT1-positive nuclei in diabetic mice compared to db/m mice (Figure 1(G,H)). These findings confirm the successful establishment of a DKD mouse model.

### Renal lipid deposition in the glomeruli and podocytes of db/db mice

Renal lipid deposition in glomeruli and podocytes of db/db mice was examined to investigate the mechanism of podocyte injury and the role of lipid disturbances in diabetes. To assess whether hyperglycemia leads to changes in lipid metabolism, LDs were visualized using Oil red O (ORO) staining and BODIPY staining. Positive staining was observed in podocytes and the glomeruli from diabetic mice (Figure 2(A,B)). Moreover, lipid peroxidation was assessed via determining the levels of MDA, a metabolite of lipid peroxidation. A significant increase in the concentration of FFA, and MDA was detected in the glomeruli of db/db mice (Figure 2(C,D)). Sample size (n = 6/group) was based on preliminary data and power calculation [5]. In addition, ROS levels in the glomeruli of db/db mice were also significantly increased (Figure 2(E)), suggesting the increased oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation in podocytes of diabetic mice, resulting in an increase in lipid peroxidation and cell injury.

*Figure 2.: Dysfunction of glomerular lipid metabolism in DKD mice. (A) Oil red O (ORO) staining of glomeruli suggested that the accumulation of lipid droplets in glomeruli of DKD mice increased (n = 6). (B) BODIPY (green, 493/503) and immunofluorescence of WT1 (red) staining of glomeruli (n = 6). DAPI (blue) was used for nuclear staining. (C) Quantitative analyses of lipid peroxidation MDA in different groups (n = 6). (D) Quantitative analyses of glomerular FFA (n = 6). (E) Quantitative analyses of glomerular ROS levels in different groups (n = 6). **p < 0.01 and ***p < 0.001. Five visual fields for each section analyzed.*

### Alteration in the expression of LRH-1 and PLIN5 in db/db mice

To gain additional insight into the underlying metabolic program required for LDs accumulation, the glomerular transcriptome was analyzed by RNA-Seq (Figure 3(A)). Intriguingly, the expression of PLIN5, a key regulator of lipid metabolism by approximating LDs and mitochondria, was downregulated in the glomeruli of db/db mice (Figure 3(A)). Given the potential regulatory mechanism of LRH-1 on PLIN5 was revealed in other metabolic tissues in lipid mobilization, we assessed the expression of LRH-1 in the renal tissues of mice. Kidneys were then extracted, and protein lysate was generated from the cortex. Western blots showed that both LRH-1 and PLIN5 were significantly decreased in db/db mice (Figure 3(B)). Subsequently, immunohistochemical staining, together with double labeling IF, confirmed this observation (Figure 3(C–F)).

(B) Western blot assay showing expression of LRH-1 and PLIN5 among different treatment groups and quantitative analyses of Western blot assay (n = 6). (E, F) Representative immunofluorescence staining of LRH-1 and PLIN5 with WT1 positive podocytes in glomerulus from renal tissues among different groups (n = 6). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, and ***p < 0.001. Five visual fields for each section analyzed.*

### LRH-1/PLIN5 axis in podocytes was suppressed in vitro

Next, we sought to examine the lipid metabolism changes that might occur in cultured podocytes. In consistent with in vivo studies, HG stimulation led to an increase in LDs deposition in podocytes (Figure 4(A)). In addition, podocytes subjected to HG showed a significant increase in the intracellular content of FFA, ROS, and MDA (Figure 4(B–D)). As expected, HG-treated podocytes exhibited a significant decrease in LRH-1 and PLIN5, as shown by Western blot (Figure 4(E)). Since previous works have identified that LRH-1 regulates the transcription of PLIN5, and the expression of LRH-1 is responsible for the homeostasis of the lipid metabolic process. Using PROMO, a transcription factor binding site prediction program, we analyzed the upstream promoter sequence of PLIN5 and identified multiple putative LRH-1 binding sites (Figure 4(F)). Protein–nucleic acid docking substantiated the hypothesis that LRH-1 influences PLIN5 transcription through the sequence ‘GTCATT’ (Figure 4(G)). Luciferase and Western blot analyses demonstrated that mutating this sequence effectively reversed LRH-1’s transcriptional regulation (Figure 4(G–I)). Altogether, these results substantiated the presumptive role of LRH-1 in regulating PLIN5 expression in podocytes. To further confirm the direct transcriptional regulation of PLIN5 by LRH‑1, we analyzed public LRH‑1 ChIP‑seq data from multiple cell lines (Supplementary Figure S3). Consistent enrichment of LRH‑1 was observed at the PLIN5 promoter region harboring the conserved GTCATT motif, indicating a cell‑type‑independent binding pattern. In addition, co‑immunoprecipitation (Co‑IP) assays showed no direct protein–protein interaction between LRH‑1 and PLIN5 (Supplementary Figures S4 and S5), supporting that LRH‑1 regulates PLIN5 at the transcriptional level rather than through direct binding.

### Upregulation of LRH-1 expression improved HG-induced lipotoxicity by promoting lipid droplet turnover

Given the role of PLIN5 in lipid metabolism, we investigated whether LRH-1 could regulate LD turnover in podocytes. As expected, transfection of LRH-1 plasmid into podocytes attenuated HG-induced LDs accumulation (Figure 5(A–D)), and reduced the intracellular content of FFA, MDA, and ROS levels in podocytes (Figure 5(E–G)). To further reveal the regulation mechanisms, we investigated the presence of LDs under different conditions. Interestingly, HG stimulation reduced the contact of LDs to mitochondria, but increased the co-localization of LDs and lysosomes in podocytes, indicating an increased lipid flux to lysosomes for degradation (Figure 5(H,I)). In contrast, upregulation of LRH-1 markedly increased the colocalization of LDs and mitochondria, inhibited lysosomal lipolysis, and suggested that more lipids entered the mitochondrial utilization pathway (Figure 5(H,I)). Together with the results above, we demonstrate that HG stimulation caused the imbalance between lipolysis and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, excessive accumulation of lipotoxic substances caused podocyte injury, and LRH-1 inhibited the lipolysis overactivation by promoting the expression of PLIN5, and increased the utilization of LDs, thus avoiding lipotoxicity.

### DLPC administration enhanced the expression of LRH-1 and PLIN5 and alleviated renal damage in db/db mice

To explore the therapeutic potential of LRH-1 activation, we treated db/db mice with DLPC, an LRH-1 agonist (Figure 6(A)). The administration of DLPC to db/db mice resulted in a reduction in body weight, blood glucose, and UACR levels (Figure 6(B–D)). Furthermore, DLPC treatment also led to improvements in loss of foot processes of podocytes, expansion of the mesangial matrix, marked sclerosis of glomeruli, and glomerular lipid accumulation in db/db mice (Figure 6(E,F)). Furthermore, glomerular proteins were prepared for Western blot analysis (Figure 6(G–I)). As shown in Figure 6(J–M), the administration of DLPC markedly elevated the expression of LRH-1 and PLIN5 in the glomeruli of db/db mice in comparison to those of db/db mice, as demonstrated by IF co-staining of podocytes. These findings suggest that the activation of LRH-1 may mitigate renal injury in the DKD state by enhancing PLIN5-mediated lipid metabolism.

### CA upregulated PLIN5 expression and ameliorated renal lipid accumulation in db/db mice

To identify a therapeutic agent targeting PLIN5 in podocytes, we screened natural compounds from traditional Chinese medicines. Several studies have identified natural compounds derived from traditional Chinese medicines that have demonstrated significant therapeutic value in the long-term treatment of DKD. Consequently, we proceeded to identify the five PLIN5 protein-targeting candidates with the highest docking scores through virtual screening of the Natural Products Library database (Figure 7(A)). These were tetragalloylglucose, cistanoside A, CA, tubuloside A, and poliumoside (Figure 7(B)). Further functional analysis, conducted using BODIPY and ORO staining, revealed that CA had the most pronounced effect on improving lipid accumulation in HG-induced podocytes (Figure 7(C,D)). Furthermore, the Western blot results confirmed that CA had the most pronounced up-regulation of PLIN5, indicating that CA is a promising PLIN5 agonist (Figure 7(E)). Additionally, following the administration of CA to db/db mice via intraperitoneal injection, improvements in body weight, blood glucose, and UACR levels were observed in db/db mice (Figure 7(F–I)). Of note, CA treatment significantly upregulated PLIN5 expression, ameliorated lipid accumulation, and renal injury (Figure 7(J,K)). Collectively, these results confirm that CA can ameliorate renal injury and lipid accumulation in db/db mice by upregulating PLIN5.

## Discussion

Podocytes play a crucial role in the maintenance of the glomerular filtration barrier, and their damage is closely associated with the onset and progression of DKD [23]. Fatty acid metabolism is indispensable for maintaining the energy supply, membrane structural integrity, and oxidative stress balance in podocytes [24]. Lipids, as high-energy-density molecules, are essential for the energy provision to podocytes. Podocytes generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) through fatty acid oxidation to meet their metabolic demands [25]. When the activity of fatty acid oxidation declines, the insufficient energy supply to podocytes leads to apoptosis and the disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier [26]. Additionally, the present finding indicates that in a HG environment, excess lipids, FFA, and lipid metabolites were detected in podocytes, further exacerbating apoptosis and damage to the filtration barrier, consistent with our previous findings [5,27].

Based on the observed reduction in intracellular FFAs and lipid accumulation, lipid metabolism may be associated with the maintenance of foot process structure and membrane properties in podocytes [28]. Dysregulation of fatty acid metabolism can lead to abnormal membrane structures, adversely affecting podocyte filtration function and signal transduction, thereby promoting pathological changes [29]. Under scanning electron microscopy, we observed the disappearance of foot process structures, indicative of lipotoxic damage in a HG environment. Proper fatty acid oxidation can eliminate ROS and maintain the intracellular redox balance. However, both excessive and insufficient fatty acid oxidation can lead to ROS accumulation, causing oxidative stress and damaging the structure and function of podocytes. Our findings are in strong accord with these mechanisms.

Our study revealed that LRH-1 has a protective effect on podocytes under HG conditions, with its overexpression promoting fatty acid oxidative metabolism. Previous research has shown that the absence of PLIN5 leads to apoptosis, oxidative stress, and inflammation in podocytes with HG stimulation [30]. Our study further confirmed this observation, noting that overexpression of LRH-1 or the use of LRH-1 agonists could upregulate PLIN5 expression, while podocytes with low PLIN5 expression exhibited higher lipid accumulation.

PLIN5, an essential functional protein localized to the surface of LDs, serves as a critical regulator of intracellular lipid homeostasis [31]. Its primary physiological role involves maintaining LD stability and orchestrating the delicate balance between lipid storage and mobilization [32]. PLIN5 is indispensable for the structural integrity of LDs; research indicates that the absence of PLIN5 leads to LD instability, which subsequently impairs cellular lipid metabolic flux [33]. Beyond structural maintenance, PLIN5 acts as a metabolic scaffold that modulates the activity of lipases, such as adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL), on the LD surface. This regulation is vital for the controlled release and reutilization of fatty acids, particularly under conditions of heightened metabolic demand, including exercise or fasting [34,35]. Historically, while PLIN1 is recognized as the predominant perilipin in white adipose tissue (WAT), the distribution of PLIN5 is distinctively concentrated in tissues characterized by high oxidative capacity. Studies have demonstrated that PLIN5 is most highly expressed in the heart, skeletal muscle, and liver, as well as in brown adipose tissue (BAT) – sites where rapid lipid turnover and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation are central to energy homeostasis [31]. The enrichment of PLIN5 in these oxidative environments underscores its specialized role in facilitating the efficient transfer of fatty acids from LDs to mitochondria.

Importantly, our study demonstrates that PLIN5 is a transcriptional target of LRH‑1 in podocytes. Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assays verified no direct protein–protein interaction between LRH-1 and PLIN5, confirming that LRH-1 regulates PLIN5 at the transcriptional rather than post-translational level. The binding of LRH‑1 to the PLIN5 promoter is highly conserved across cell types. Analysis of public LRH‑1 ChIP‑seq datasets confirmed robust and specific enrichment at the PLIN5 promoter region containing the GTCATT motif in multiple cell lines, independent of cellular context. This cross‑cell consistency validates that the GTCATT motif is a bona fide LRH‑1 response element and strengthens the conclusion that LRH‑1 directly controls PLIN5 transcription in podocytes. This finding suggests a novel regulatory axis in the kidney, where PLIN5 may play a pivotal role in protecting podocytes from lipotoxic injury by managing lipid mobilization and metabolic health.

Lipid droplet turnover, interacting with mitochondria, maintains energy homeostasis, regulates lipid metabolism, and participates in cell signaling, vital for cell function and survival [36,37]. LDs primarily store energy, while mitochondria are the cell’s powerhouses, responsible for energy production [38]. The interaction between these two structures is of paramount importance for the survival and function of podocytes [13,39]. First, the interplay between mitochondria and LDs helps to maintain energy metabolism balance. During high energy demand, fatty acids are released from LDs to generate ATP, thus meeting the cell’s energy needs [39]. For podocytes, maintaining the balance of energy supply is fundamental to their normal function. Based on our colocalization analysis, the spatial proximity between LDs and mitochondria may be associated with the regulation of oxidative stress. Mitochondria are the main sites of ROS production, and excessive ROS can potentially cause oxidative damage to cells. It should be emphasized that these observations reflect only morphological and protein expression changes and do not directly demonstrate functional lipid flux or causal relationships. Through dynamic interactions with mitochondria, LDs can absorb and neutralize some ROS, thereby protecting podocytes from oxidative stress to a certain extent. Lastly, the interplay between LDs and mitochondria also affects podocyte signal transduction. Many metabolic pathways and signaling molecules may be involved in the interactions between these two subcellular structures. For example, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is an essential energy sensor that coordinates the functions of LDs and mitochondria, thus influencing the cell’s metabolic state and survival [40]. In the present study, we identified that HG stimulation reduced the contact of LDs with mitochondria, but increased lysosomal degradation of LDs, resulting in increased release of FFA [5,41]. The interaction between LRH-1 and PLIN5 plays a pivotal role in this process. LRH-1 promotes the homeostasis between LDs and mitochondria by activating the expression of PLIN5. Meanwhile, PLIN5 regulates the dynamic balance of LDs by preventing their degradation through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway and by interacting with lipid-degrading enzymes. In addition, we confirmed these findings through the application of LRH-1 agonist DLPC and the selected molecule compound CA, which also provide clues for the development of agents targeting the LRH-1/PLIN5 axis.

## Conclusions

In conclusion, LDs play a critical role in cellular metabolism and homeostasis through their interactions with mitochondria. These interactions are especially important for maintaining cellular health and preventing lipid accumulation. We hypothesize that LRH-1 may modify LDs metabolism by regulating PLIN5, providing a new mechanism and therapeutic target for lipid toxicity-induced damage in diabetic podocytes. This opens new avenues for future research and clinical treatment, which will help to improve the prognosis of patients with diabetic nephropathy.
